lesson.title: Estimating Error Before You Measure It: The Differential Approximation
lesson.summary: Combining dy and dx gives f(a + dx) is approximately f(a) + dy, a one-line way to estimate how a small change or measurement error in an input propagates into the output.
lesson.body:
Putting dy and dx together with the error awareness from a few chapters back produces the differential approximation: f(a + dx) is approximately f(a) + dy, where dy = f'(a) dx. This is true almost by construction, since dy was defined to make it true, but it is worth stating on its own because of how it gets used: whenever dx is small, the approximation is trustworthy, and when dx grows, the error chapter's warnings about distance and curvature apply.

The most common use of this idea is propagating measurement error. If an input can only be measured to within some small tolerance, the differential approximation estimates how much error that tolerance creates in a quantity computed from it, without recomputing the full formula from scratch.

Here is a classic version of that problem. A sphere's volume is V(r) = (4/3) pi r^3. Suppose a ball bearing's radius is measured as r = 5 cm, but the measuring instrument is only accurate to within dr = 0.1 cm. Since dV/dr = 4 pi r^2, the differential estimate of the resulting volume error is dV = 4 pi (5)^2 (0.1) = 4 pi (25)(0.1) = 10 pi, which is about 31.416 cubic centimeters. Checking against the exact change confirms this is a good estimate: V(5.1) - V(5) = (4/3) pi (5.1^3 - 5^3) = (4/3) pi (132.651 - 125) = (4/3) pi (7.651), which works out to about 32.048 cubic centimeters. The differential estimate of 31.416 is within about 0.63 cubic centimeters of the true change, an error of roughly two percent, small enough that the quick estimate can be trusted without redoing the full cubic calculation.

This is exactly the pattern that economics reuses in the next chapters, just with a specific, very natural choice of dx: one more unit of whatever is being produced. Fixing dx = 1 turns the differential approximation into what economists call marginal analysis.
